questions.prompt: Antibody opsonization and complement opsonization (Module 21) both enhance phagocytosis. What is the key difference?

options.text: Complement is made by plasma cells, so it is just as specific as the antibodies are
Only complement uses phagocyte receptors; antibodies need no receptors to mark pathogens
Only antibodies can cause lysis; complement can only coat pathogens for phagocytosis
Antibodies mark specific pathogens; mannose/LPS-triggered complement marks them nonspecifically

questions.explanation: Both use phagocyte receptors (constant region vs C3b).

why.A: Complement isn't made by plasma cells.
why.C: Complement can lyse via the MAC.

questions.prompt: A patient's IgE binds pollen on mast cells. Which Module 20 events follow?

options.text: Phagocytosis of the mast cell by macrophages → pus forms → healing
MAC formation on pollen grains → pollen lysis → fever and chills
Interferon release → neighboring cells make AVPs → pollen RNA destroyed
Histamine → vasodilation and leaky vessels → redness, heat, swelling, pain

questions.prompt: Which statement about B cells is FALSE?

options.text: Each B cell can make antibodies with many different binding sites.
Memory B cells keep their receptors.
A B cell can make different classes of antibody with the same binding site.
The B cell receptor is a membrane-bound IgM monomer.
B cells mature in the bone marrow.

questions.explanation: Each B cell makes only one kind of binding site.

why.B: True — memory B cells keep receptors.
why.C: True — class can switch with the same site.
why.D: True — BCR is an IgM monomer.
why.E: True — B cells mature in bone marrow.

questions.prompt: A vaccine's goal, in Module 22 terms, is to:

options.text: Create memory cells in advance so real exposure acts like a secondary response
Prevent clonal selection so B cells don't overreact to the pathogen
Activate IgE on mast cells so inflammation starts faster next time
Give preformed antibodies that protect for a few weeks with no memory

questions.prompt: Why is antivenom given rather than waiting for the victim's immune response?

options.text: Antivenom creates memory cells that last for the rest of life
A primary response takes about a week; venom acts much faster
Snakebite victims are unable to make antibodies against venom
Venom isn't an antigen, so B cells can never recognize it

why.C: Victims can make antibodies, just slowly.

questions.prompt: Which observation would show that IgA in breast milk mainly protects by neutralization?

options.text: It forms a membrane attack complex on gut bacteria
It blocks pathogens and toxins from attaching to the gut lining
It causes mast cells in the infant's gut to burst open
It crosses into the infant's blood and creates memory cells

why.D: IgA stays in the gut and gives no memory.

questions.prompt: Why are several antibody defense mechanisms described as not mutually exclusive?

options.text: The same bound antibodies can neutralize, opsonize, and agglutinate at once
Only IgG can perform more than one mechanism; all others do just one
Each antibody can perform only one mechanism during its whole lifetime
The mechanisms always happen in a fixed order, one after the other

questions.explanation: One binding event does several jobs.

questions.prompt: Which change on a titer graph after a second exposure most reflects memory B cells?

options.text: The lag phase before antibodies gets longer
The IgM curve becomes several times higher
The IgG curve rises sooner and far higher
The IgG curve disappears and only IgM remains

questions.explanation: Many memory cells → many plasma cells → lots of IgG.

why.B: IgG, not IgM, rises much higher.

questions.prompt: Which antigen fact from the slides matters for clonal selection?

options.text: One pathogen can show many antigens, each selecting different B cells
Antigens are made by B cells and then displayed on the pathogen
Each pathogen has exactly one antigen, so only one B cell responds
Antigens must be made of DNA to be recognized by B cell receptors

why.B: Antigens aren't made by B cells.
why.D: Antigens are often proteins, not DNA.

questions.prompt: Which mother-to-child transfer happens after the umbilical cord is cut?

options.text: IgG through the placenta
IgE through skin contact
IgM through the placenta
IgA through breast milk

questions.explanation: IgG transfer ends at birth; breastfeeding continues protection.

questions.prompt: Which pair of cells both come from a selected B cell?

options.text: Neutrophils and macrophages
Mast cells and eosinophils
Plasma cells and memory B cells
Helper and cytotoxic T cells

why.D: T cells come from the thymus.

questions.prompt: A drug destroyed all memory B cells. What would happen at the next exposure to a previously defeated pathogen?

options.text: Nothing would change, because plasma cells would still be ready
It would look like a primary response, with a lag and likely illness
IgE on mast cells would take over and replace the antibody response
Passive immunity from the mother would automatically take over

questions.explanation: Memory makes the secondary response fast.

why.D: Maternal immunity is long gone in adults.

questions.prompt: Which statement explains why passive immunity gives no memory?

options.text: Preformed antibodies destroy the recipient's B cells after injection
Memory cells can't recognize antibodies that were made somewhere else
The recipient's B cells never bind the antigen, so no clonal selection
Passive antibodies are all IgE, which can't create memory cells

questions.explanation: No selection means no memory cells.

why.A: Passive antibodies don't destroy B cells.
why.B: Memory cells come from the recipient's own B cells.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of an antibody (constant vs variable regions, two binding sites) makes agglutination, opsonization, and inflammation possible.
questions.explanation: Two identical variable-region binding sites let one antibody grab antigens on two pathogens (agglutination). The constant region binds receptors on phagocytes (opsonization) and, for IgE, on mast cells (inflammation), so universal receptors work no matter what antigen the variable region recognizes.

questions.prompt: Using clonal selection, explain why you usually get sick the first time you meet a pathogen but not the second time.
questions.explanation: First time: the rare matching B cell must be found, selected, and cloned, so antibodies take about a week — enough time for disease. Clonal expansion also makes memory B cells, so on second exposure many matching cells respond immediately, producing high IgG fast enough to clear the pathogen before illness.
